content:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-21
Time: 10:00 AM ET
Duration: 45 min
Call type: PoC check-in / weekly sync

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Stephanie Nguyen (AE), Evan Scott (SE), Fatima Noor (SE)
NorthBridge Bank: Alex Chen (Platform Eng), Priya Shah (Security Eng), Tom Gallagher (ML Eng), Rachel Li (SRE)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- The team reviewed Week 1 benchmark results for the NorthBridge PoC running in a VPC-connected setup.
- NorthBridge reported integration friction around DNS/TLS in the VPC path and questions about audit logging fields + export destinations.
- Redwood proposed tuning concurrency and batching settings and clarified how audit logs and retention controls work across Dedicated vs Private deployments.
- Next steps include Redwood sending a benchmark recap + sample audit log event, and NorthBridge providing their required audit schema and preferred export method (Splunk HEC vs S3).

Topics
1) Week 1 benchmark results (latency, throughput, error rates)
2) Integration issues (VPC networking, DNS, TLS cert chain, timeouts)
3) Logging/audit requirements (fields, export, retention)
4) Success criteria + plan for Week 2

Action items
- Redwood: send benchmark recap + config recommendations
- Redwood: provide sample audit log payload + export options
- NorthBridge: share Splunk/logging requirements + allowed egress targets
- NorthBridge: confirm required retention period and whether prompts/responses can be logged

Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Hey everyone. Alright, we’ll give it like 30 seconds. I see Alex, Priya, Tom, Rachel. Great. Evan and Fatima are on too. This is week one check-in for the PoC. Goal today is, uh, look at benchmark results, anything blocked on integration, and then specifically logging because I know Priya and Rachel had questions. Sound right?

[00:18] Alex Chen: Yep. That’s right.

[00:19] Priya Shah: Yep, and retention.

[00:21] Evan Scott: Cool. I can start with what we saw on the benchmark harness.

[00:26] Tom Gallagher: Before you do, just to level set, we ran the harness mostly with 256 output tokens because that’s what we think our summarization jobs are going to be. We can increase, but that’s where the numbers came from.

[00:36] Evan Scott: Perfect. That matches what I have.

[00:38] Evan Scott: So, Week 1 results. You’re currently pinned to the “Llama 3 70B Instruct” profile we set up, running with streaming enabled, temperature 0.2, max output 256. Requests are coming from your app tier in the PoC VPC, through the private endpoint. What we saw across the last run, which was, I think, Tuesday night?

[00:59] Rachel Li: Yeah, around 8 PM Eastern.

[01:01] Evan Scott: Right. Over 10k requests total, with a ramp from 1 RPS to 12 RPS sustained. p50 end-to-end latency was around 410 milliseconds for the first token, then total completion p50 was 1.9 seconds. p95 total completion was 3.8 seconds. We also saw a couple of spikes to 6-7 seconds during the ramp peaks.

[01:21] Tom Gallagher: That’s including network overhead and TLS handshake?

[01:25] Evan Scott: It’s end-to-end from your client. It includes the network path. We did filter out retries and timeouts. There were timeouts; we can talk about those.

[01:32] Rachel Li: Our side showed a bunch of 504s. Not a ton, but like, enough.

[01:36] Evan Scott: Exactly. Error rate was 0.7% on the run. Most of that was request timeouts at 10 seconds. The distribution suggests it’s not the model; it’s queueing during burst and then your client timeout is relatively tight for the p95 tail.

[01:52] Alex Chen: We set 10 seconds because security was like, don’t keep sockets open forever.

[01:56] Priya Shah: Not just security. We also have downstream systems that, you know, blow up if you hold threads.

[02:01] Evan Scott: Totally fair. We can do two things: tune concurrency and batching so tail improves, and also use server-side max queue time so we fail fast instead of sitting in queue.

[02:12] Fatima Noor: And for streaming, if you care about time-to-first-token, your users experience is more like the 410ms number, not the full completion time. But for batch summarization you’re going to care about total time.

[02:23] Tom Gallagher: Yeah, for the batch job it’s total. For the agent thing, it’s first token.

[02:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we pause and align on success criteria? Just to make sure we’re optimizing the right thing.

[02:33] Alex Chen: We have two. One is interactive internal support assistant, that needs under 700ms to first token p95 ideally. The other is nightly summarization and classification, and that’s basically cost and throughput. We want to do about, call it, 30 million tokens overnight.

[02:50] Evan Scott: Got it. For the interactive piece, your p95 first token was 820ms. That’s slightly above your target but close. And I think we can get it under 700 with some tuning and maybe using a smaller model variant for the agent flow.

[03:05] Tom Gallagher: We did try the 8B model quickly and quality was… not great.

[03:09] Evan Scott: Yeah, Llama 3 8B tends to get, like, hallucinate-y for compliance-y language. We can also test 70B with different quant profile, or an intermediate size if you want. But we can keep Week 2 focused on tail improvements first.

[03:25] Rachel Li: What about throughput? We were only getting about 10 to 12 RPS before it started queueing.

[03:30] Evan Scott: That’s consistent. Right now the config is conservative because we didn’t want to break latency for interactive. For batch, we can run a separate route with more aggressive batching and higher max concurrency. Redwood supports route-level config.

[03:44] Alex Chen: So basically two endpoints. One for batch, one for interactive.

[03:47] Evan Scott: Exactly. Same model, different serving policy.

[03:50] Stephanie Nguyen: That maps nicely to Dedicated vs Private too, but we’ll come back.

[03:54] Tom Gallagher: Can you talk about the spikes to six seconds? Is that from autoscaling?

[03:58] Evan Scott: Not autoscaling. In the PoC environment we have fixed capacity. Spikes were correlated with your harness opening a lot of new connections. We saw a lot of TLS renegotiation.

[04:08] Alex Chen: That might be on us. We’re using Envoy but the keepalive settings are default.

[04:12] Rachel Li: Also DNS. We had a period where the private hosted zone lookup was slow. Like 200ms sometimes.

[04:18] Evan Scott: Yep. That shows up. One suggestion is pin the endpoint via internal DNS and ensure your resolver is in the same AZ. But I don’t want to, like, hand-wave; if you share your VPC diagram we can be more precise.

[04:32] Alex Chen: We can send it. We can’t send the full thing externally, but we can redact.

[04:36] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s fine. Redacted is okay.

[04:39] Fatima Noor: On TLS, we also saw a couple handshake failures. The error looked like “unknown CA” but it was intermittent.

[04:46] Rachel Li: Yeah. That’s because we’re doing TLS inspection in some segments. It’s gross. We might disable for the PoC subnet.

[04:54] Priya Shah: It’s not gross, it’s required.

[04:56] Rachel Li: For prod it is. For PoC we can carve out.

[05:00] Priya Shah: We’ll see.

[05:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, we can park TLS inspection as a separate thread. Let’s move to logging since that’s the bigger gating item.

[05:08] Priya Shah: Yep. So we need audit logs that show: who called the API, what model, what time, and where it ran. We also need a correlation ID and ideally token counts for billing. But we cannot store prompt or response content in Splunk. At least not by default. We can store hashes.

[05:28] Evan Scott: Understood. Redwood audit logs, conceptually, are event records per request. Typical fields: request_id, timestamp, org_id, project_id, route, model, model_version, region, deployment_mode, auth subject (like API key id or SSO user), source IP if available, and usage fields like prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens. We can also include a prompt hash. Content itself can be excluded.

[05:55] Priya Shah: Is that configurable? Like a hard guarantee that prompt and response aren’t logged?

[06:00] Fatima Noor: In Private deployments, yes, because you control the logging pipeline and config. In Hosted, Redwood has internal logs for operations, but customer-facing audit logs do not include prompt content by default. We have to be careful with wording; Evan can send the exact language we use.

[06:16] Priya Shah: Okay. We need exact.

[06:19] Rachel Li: Also export. We don’t want to manually pull from a console. We need push to Splunk HEC or to S3 and we ingest.

[06:28] Evan Scott: For Private and Dedicated, we support export to customer-controlled S3-compatible storage, and we have an HTTPS webhook export option. Splunk HEC is basically an HTTPS endpoint, so that can work if egress is allowed. Alternatively, we can do S3 bucket + your side picks up.

[06:46] Alex Chen: If it’s S3, it needs to be our AWS account, and we need a role assumption story.

[06:51] Evan Scott: Yep. For Private it’s your account anyway. For Dedicated, we’d set up cross-account write with KMS. But again, we’re not trying to sell the final architecture right now—just to get the PoC unblocked.

[07:05] Priya Shah: What about retention? We need seven years for audit. Not for prompts, but for events.

[07:12] Fatima Noor: Seven years is long. In the Redwood Console we have standard retention windows—like 30 days default, longer with an enterprise retention add-on. But for regulated customers, the common pattern is export audit logs to your SIEM or archive store where you manage retention. That’s how you get to seven years without us holding it all.

[07:31] Rachel Li: That’s acceptable if the export is reliable. Like at-least-once delivery, retries, no gaps.

[07:36] Evan Scott: Yes. The exporter has retry and backoff. If delivery fails, events queue locally up to a configured limit, and you get alerts. In Private, again, you control the infra so you can size it.

[07:49] Tom Gallagher: Can we get an example payload? Because our Splunk field extraction is… picky.

[07:55] Evan Scott: Yes. I’ll send a redacted example. We also have a schema doc but it’s internal right now; we can share the relevant fields.

[08:03] Priya Shah: Also: do you log admin actions? Like model changes, route changes.

[08:08] Fatima Noor: Yep. There are control-plane audit events too: user login, role changes, API key creation, policy changes, deployment changes. Those are separate event types.

[08:21] Priya Shah: That’s required.

[08:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Priya, would you be able to send us your “minimum audit fields” list? So we can map one-to-one and not waste cycles.

[08:31] Priya Shah: Yes. I have a spreadsheet template. I’ll send.

[08:34] Rachel Li: One thing: region. You said region is in the audit log. We need to guarantee it stays in US-East for this PoC.

[08:42] Evan Scott: For the PoC route, it’s pinned. No cross-region routing. Failures would error, not failover to another region.

[08:50] Rachel Li: Okay. Because AWS Bedrock did some weird failover when we tested.

[08:54] Tom Gallagher: Azure did too.

[08:56] Evan Scott: Yep, understood. Redwood routing is policy-based and we can set “no fallback”.

[09:03] Alex Chen: Cool. Back to integration. We still have the DNS thing. And I think our app is not reusing connections.

[09:10] Evan Scott: Right. For Week 2, I propose two tracks:
1) You change client connection reuse / keepalive settings, and we rerun benchmark.
2) We set up a second route called, like, /batch-summarize with higher batching and concurrency, and you run your nightly style load shape.

[09:30] Tom Gallagher: Can we do the second without messing up the first? Like separate quotas.

[09:34] Evan Scott: Yes, separate limits.

[09:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Rachel, from an observability standpoint, do you have enough data now to see where time is spent? Or do we need to add tracing headers.

[09:46] Rachel Li: We can see end-to-end. We’d like a server timing header if possible. Also a request_id echoed back so we can correlate with your audit log.

[09:55] Evan Scott: We already return x-request-id. But I saw sometimes it wasn’t propagated through your gateway.

[10:02] Alex Chen: That’s on us. We strip unknown headers. We’ll add it.

[10:06] Fatima Noor: We can also add server timing. I’ll check what’s supported by the gateway.

[10:12] Priya Shah: Another question. KMS. We need customer-managed keys for anything at rest.

[10:19] Fatima Noor: For Private, yes, you can use your own KMS/HSM because it’s in your environment. For Dedicated, we support KMS integration; specifics depend on cloud and setup. For Hosted, we use provider-managed encryption with optional customer-managed keys in some cases, but I don’t want to overpromise on this call. We’ll follow up with the approved statement.

[10:41] Priya Shah: Please do.

[10:43] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, we’ll keep claims tight.

[10:46] Tom Gallagher: Cost. Did you compute cost per million tokens based on the run?

[10:51] Evan Scott: We can approximate. In the run you used 92 million total tokens. The effective throughput was ~180 tokens/sec on average for that route. But cost depends on pricing model and whether Dedicated/Private. In Hosted it’s per-token. For Dedicated it’s basically capacity cost. Stephanie can cover commercial later.

[11:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Yeah, for now we’re focusing on “does it work” and “do we hit SLOs”. If we move to procurement we’ll bring in the right pricing construct.

[11:20] Alex Chen: For “does it work” we also need the security evidence pack. Not today, but soon.

[11:25] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We can start that request process. We have a regulated workloads security FAQ and an evidence pack index. It’s under NDA and controlled sharing. Priya, I’ll follow up offline to align on what you need.

[11:42] Priya Shah: Okay.

[11:44] Rachel Li: Back on the 504s. Are you seeing queue depth? Because we’re not.

[11:48] Evan Scott: Yes. In Redwood Console you can see queue time and batch size. For your route, queue time p95 hit 1.2 seconds during bursts. That’s the main cause of tail. If we allow slightly bigger batch sizes, we can increase throughput and reduce queue time.

[12:04] Tom Gallagher: Bigger batches usually increase latency, right?

[12:08] Evan Scott: It increases per-request compute time slightly, but because queue drops, p95 can improve. It’s a tradeoff. For interactive route we’ll be conservative; for batch route we’ll be aggressive.

[12:21] Alex Chen: What about max context? We’re sending 6k tokens sometimes.

[12:25] Evan Scott: For 70B, 8k context is okay; above that tail gets worse. If you’re sending 6k input, your time-to-first-token will go up. In the harness, you were at about 1.2k input average.

[12:39] Tom Gallagher: That’s good to know. Our real prompts can be bigger.

[12:42] Fatima Noor: We should sample from your real distribution. Even if you can’t share raw prompts, you can share token lengths and maybe synthetic prompts with same length.

[12:52] Priya Shah: We can share token lengths.

[12:54] Evan Scott: Great. That’ll help us tune kernel selection and caching.

[13:00] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to make sure we capture the integration blockers. Alex, what’s the biggest thing right now?

[13:06] Alex Chen: Biggest is getting the private endpoint stable with our DNS and cert chain. Second is logging export. Third is—maybe SSO, but that’s later.

[13:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Logging export is on our action list. DNS/TLS, we’ll take the diagram and do a shorter troubleshooting session if needed.

[13:25] Rachel Li: Can we do that tomorrow? Because we need to rerun the benchmark by Friday.

[13:30] Evan Scott: Tomorrow works for me. 30 minutes.

[13:33] Stephanie Nguyen: I’ll have my assistant send times.

[13:36] Priya Shah: One more logging question. Do you log “deny” events? Like blocked requests.

[13:42] Fatima Noor: Yes, policy decisions can be logged. For example, if a request violates a route policy (region mismatch, auth failure, rate limit) you get an audit event with outcome=denied and reason.

[13:54] Priya Shah: Good.

[13:56] Tom Gallagher: On the benchmark recap, can you include “time to first token” p95? That’s the one my VP cares about.

[14:02] Evan Scott: Yep, I’ll include TTFT p50/p95 and total completion.

[14:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Before we wrap, quick recap of Week 2 plan:
- Two routes: interactive and batch
- Customer adjusts keepalive/header propagation
- Redwood sends audit log sample and benchmark recap
- We do a DNS/TLS troubleshooting session

Anything I missed?

[14:25] Alex Chen: Also, we need confirmation the route is pinned to US-East and no fallback.

[14:30] Evan Scott: I’ll put it in writing in the recap.

[14:33] Priya Shah: And exact wording on retention and whether you store prompts.

[14:37] Fatima Noor: Yep, we’ll send approved language.

[14:40] Rachel Li: And if possible, a way to export metrics too, not just audit logs. Prometheus scrape or something.

[14:47] Evan Scott: In Private, Prometheus is standard. In Dedicated, we can provide metrics export depending on setup. For PoC, we can give you CSV exports from Console; but I get that’s not ideal.

[15:02] Rachel Li: Okay, we’ll take CSV for now.

[15:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. Evan and Fatima will follow up with the docs by end of day tomorrow. We’ll schedule the DNS/TLS session. Same time next week for Week 2 check-in?

[15:16] Alex Chen: Works.

[15:17] Priya Shah: Works.

[15:18] Tom Gallagher: Yep.

[15:19] Rachel Li: Yep.

[15:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Talk soon.

(Transcript continues with light small talk for ~30 seconds; recording ends.)
